summary: Nutrition is the weakest part of the setup, and the KB has the priority wrong. Its own numbers don't add up: a weighed intake of 1800–2000 kcal against its own TDEE estimate of 2600–2900 is a 23–38 % deficit, not a "mild" one, and that doesn't square with "weight stable". If the weighed intake is correct, energy availability is about 17–21 kcal/kg FFM now and would fall to 12–18 as volume rises to 55–70 km. That is low-energy-availability territory. The ~240–250 g carb figure isn't measured either. It is what's left over from assumed totals, and the documented menu only explains ~100–120 g of it. Carbs, not fat, are the main gap: the athlete needs about 4–7 g/kg by phase versus ~2.5–3 g/kg now. Race fueling practice has to start with the main block in October, not in March 2027. Long runs pass 2 h from November and the marathon needs 60–90 g/h. The strength philosophy is sound, but the gym schedules in 09 and 04 contradict each other and the errata. The program is also missing soleus/Achilles loading, plyometrics and hip work, which a heavy runner needs most, and it has no plan for travel or the ski trip. Sleep, the protein correction and long-run durability are good. The aerobic plateau from July to September cannot be tied to low energy availability, because summer heat and the volume increase explain it at least as well.

findings.title: The energy numbers don't reconcile: the deficit is not 'mild', and at the logged intake energy availability is already low
findings.claim: The KB states intake 1800–2000 kcal (weighed), TDEE 2600–2900, 'mírný deficit' and 'váha stabilní'. These cannot all be true. Using the KB's own TDEE, the deficit is 600–1100 kcal/day (23–38 %). That should produce 0.55–1.0 kg/week of weight loss, which isn't happening. A per-component estimate of TDEE is higher still. So either real average intake is higher than the weekday figure (weekends, celebrations, unweighed items), or energy expenditure has adapted downward, which is itself a low-energy-availability response. If the intake is accurate, energy availability is already in the LEA range and gets worse as the plan adds volume, because 07:73 only raises the target to 2400–2600 kcal. The July–September aerobic plateau cannot be pinned on this: it overlaps the summer heat and the volume rising from ~20 to 38 km.
findings.evidence: KB: 07_nutrition.md:5 (1800–2000 weighed; errata 11:48-51), 07:66 (TDEE 2600–2900), 07:73 (2400–2600 at 45–55 km), 01_athlete_profile.md:6-7 (mild deficit, weight stable). Running energy from weekly.json at ~1 kcal/kg/km × 83 kg: week 7.9. 38.6 km = 3204 kcal (458/day); week 14.9. 37.7 km = 3129 kcal (447/day). Per-component TDEE (RMR 1800–2100 for 83 kg/29 y, height unknown; NEAT 400–600 for 10–15k steps; running 0.95 kcal/kg/km; 3 gym sessions × ~175 kcal net; 10 % TEF): ~3000–3550 kcal at 38 km/week, 3200–3750 at 55 km, 3400–3950 at 70 km. A conservative lower bound (RMR 1700, NEAT 300) gives ~2780. Energy availability = (intake − exercise energy)/FFM, with FFM assumed 68–73 kg (body composition unknown, 12:32) and gym at 250 kcal/session: now 17.0–21.2 kcal/kg FFM; at 44 km (3.–9.11.) 16.0–20.2; at 55 km (Dec) 14.3–18.2; at 70 km (Apr) 12.3–16.2. LEA threshold is <30. It is less defined in men, but months below ~25 are linked to lower testosterone and fT3 and to bone stress. Plateau check (easy/long runs, tests excluded): monthly median EF_gap Jul 1.161 (n=12), Aug 1.140 (n=11), Sep 1.162 (n=11); GAP pace at HR 143–150: 5:52 / 6:00 / 5:54. That is flat since July, but confounded by heat and the volume ramp.
findings.recommendation: (1) Eat to maintenance in Indonesia; don't count. (2) Run a 14-day audit on return, 13.–26.10.: daily morning weight (after toilet, before food) as a 7-day average, plus complete weighed logging including weekends, alcohol, gels and eating out. Real TDEE = average intake + (change in 7-day weight in kg × 7700 / days). (3) Don't wait for the audit to change direction. From 13.10. start at ~2600–2800 kcal, with the +600–800 mostly from carbs, then titrate. If the 7-day average falls >0.3 kg/week unintentionally, add 200 kcal. If it rises >0.3 kg/week after the first week (the first week's rise is glycogen and water), remove 200. Scaling rule: each extra 10 km/week needs ~+120 kcal/day, so expect ~2900–3300 kcal at 55 km and ~3200–3600 at 65–70 km. (4) Red flags that mean +300–500 kcal immediately and a doctor or blood test: weight stable while intake is truly <2200; lower libido or fewer morning erections; overnight resting HR up >5 bpm on a 7-day average; repeated colds; focal bone pain; easy-run EF not improving in cool October–November weather. (5) Log resting HR from the watch's overnight data (12:29 lists it as unmeasured).
findings.plan_change: Add a 'Výživa' row to each block in 04: Indonesia = maintenance, no counting; 13.10.–26.10. = audit plus 2600–2800 kcal; 45–55 km = ~2900–3300; marathon block 60–70 km = ~3200–3600, with titration by 7-day weight. Also rewrite 07:64-73 (drop 'mírný deficit' and the 2400–2600 target), change 01:6 to 'deficit neověřený, energie nesedí', and change 12:61 from 'od 45+ km maintenance' to 'maintenance od 13.10.'

findings.title: The ~240–250 g carb figure is a leftover calculation, not a measurement, and carbs (not fat) are the main gap
findings.claim: 07:6 and 07:59 get carbs by subtracting assumed protein and fat from an assumed 2000 kcal. At 1800 kcal the same arithmetic gives 180–215 g (2.2–2.6 g/kg). The documented menu's carb sources only explain ~100–120 g. Following the errata, this is not a claim about true intake; it means the carb number has never been verified. Even at face value, ~3 g/kg is the bottom of the range for light training. At the planned 5.5–7 h/week of running it is roughly half of what the evidence supports. The KB ranks fat as the 'hlavní problém'. Fat at 25–30 g really is low, but fixing fat while keeping kcal the same (12:10, 'move calories into fats') would push carbs to ~180 g (2.2 g/kg).
findings.evidence: KB: 07:6 ('zbytek sacharidy ~240–250 g'), 07:59 (residual arithmetic), 07:8-14 (menu), 07:16 ('Hlavní problém: TUKY'), 08:9, 12:9-10. Residual arithmetic: 1800 kcal with P180–200/F25–30 gives C = 182–214 g; 2000 kcal gives 232–264 g. Menu carb sources by food tables: 50 g oats ≈ 30 g, 2 × 25 g dry rice noodles ≈ 40 g, 500 g vegetables ≈ 25 g, 250 g tvaroh ≈ 9 g, sauces and whey ≈ 10 g, total ≈ 100–120 g. Targets (IOC/ACSM 2016, Burke 2011): ~1 h/day moderate training 5–7 g/kg; 1–3 h/day 6–10 g/kg. For 83 kg: 4 g/kg = 332 g, 5 = 415 g, 6 = 498 g, 7 = 581 g, 8–10 = 664–830 g. With P175 g and F65 g, total kcal would be 2613 at 4 g/kg, 2945 at 5 g/kg and 3277 at 6 g/kg, which matches the maintenance range in N1.
findings.recommendation: Get the weighed 7-day macro totals from the tracking app before planning on any carb number. Then periodize. Indonesia: eat to appetite, rice-based, ~3.5–4.5 g/kg. 13.10.–23.11. (28–52 km): easy and rest days 3.5–4 g/kg (290–330 g); threshold or hill day 5 g/kg (~415 g); long-run day and the day before any long run ≥16 km 6 g/kg (~500 g). December (55 km, two quality sessions): average 5–6 g/kg. Marathon block (58–70 km): average 5–7 g/kg, and 7–8 g/kg on and before long runs ≥26 km. Race: 36–48 h carb-load at 8–10 g/kg (660–830 g/day), low fiber. Practical: the current 500 g vegetables plus 500 g chicken per day is very filling, so on key days swap part of the vegetables for rice, pasta, potatoes or bread, and add bananas, juice or honey. Have 30–60 g carbs before threshold sessions. Raise fat to 60–70 g as an addition to total kcal, not a swap. Protein at 170–180 g (errata) is right; don't go higher.
findings.plan_change: Add a carb g/kg line per block in 04: main block weeks 1–6 4–5 g/kg average with 6 g/kg on long-run days; weeks 8–10 5–6; marathon block 5–7; race week 8–10 g/kg for 36–48 h. Rewrite 07:57-62 as a g/kg table. Change 07:16 and 08:9 to 'Hlavní problém: celková energie a sacharidy; tuky až #2'.

findings.title: Race-fueling practice must start in October 2026, not 8.3.2027, and the target is 60–90 g/h, not one gel every 30–40 min
findings.claim: 12:49-50 postpones fueling tests to the March MP long runs. The gut adapts over weeks of repeated practice, and the long runs pass 2 h in November. The 07 gel table gives only ~35–50 g/h. For an 83 kg runner the marathon is a big carbohydrate problem. It costs ~3500 kcal, and if MP stays close to threshold, a large share of that comes from carbs. Stored glycogen does not cover it without ≥60 g/h during the race. The extra muscle glycogen of a bodybuilder's upper body cannot be used by the legs, because muscle cannot release its glycogen into the blood.
findings.evidence: KB: 12:49-50 ('Testovat od bloku 8.3.2027'), 07:113-117 ('120+ min: 1 gel každých 30–40 min', ≈ 37–50 g/h with 25 g gels), 07:125-126; README: gels tested once (28.6., 13.19 km, one gel after 5 km). Long-run durations from 04:88-97 and 04:156-164 at 6:10/km: 18 km = 1:51 (3.–9.11.), 20 km = 2:03, 22 km = 2:15 (1.–7.12.), 24 km = 2:28, 28 km = 2:52, 32 km = 3:17. Marathon at 4:58/km = 3:29:40. Energy 42.2 km × 83 kg × ~1 kcal/kg/km ≈ 3500 kcal; at 65–85 % from carbs that is 570–740 g. Race intake over 3.5 h: 60 g/h = 210 g, 75 g/h = 262 g, 90 g/h = 315 g. Evidence: gut training raises oxidation of ingested carbs and cuts GI symptoms within 2–4 weeks (Cox 2010; Costa 2017); >60 g/h needs glucose plus fructose (Jeukendrup 2014).
findings.recommendation: Use every long run ≥75 min for gut training. 13.10.–2.11. (long runs 12–17 km): ~30–40 g/h, first gel at ~40 min, 300–500 ml/h fluid. 3.–23.11. (18–21 km): 45–60 g/h, a gel every 25–30 min from minute 30. Have the vest bought by 3.11. (10:15-19). December (22–24 km): a fixed 60 g/h; start testing 2:1 glucose:fructose products and whatever gel the race will hand out. January long runs 18–22 km: 60–75 g/h. Marathon block: 60–90 g/h, including during MP segments, because gut tolerance falls at race intensity. Test caffeine twice (N9). Rehearse a full carb-load before the half marathon (29.3.–4.4.) and before one 30–32 km peak long run (5.–18.4.). Race: breakfast of 1–2 g/kg (80–160 g carbs) 2.5–3 h before the start, then 60–90 g/h (~8–12 gels of 25 g, fewer if larger), sodium 300–600 mg/h, drinking to thirst at ~400–800 ml/h and never more than ~1 L/h.
findings.plan_change: Add a 'fueling na LR' column to the 04 main-block table: weeks 1–3 30–40 g/h, weeks 4–6 45–60, weeks 7–10 60 g/h. In the marathon block, add 60–90 g/h, a caffeine test in week 5 (15.–21.3.) and at the half marathon, and carb-load rehearsals before the half and before the week-8 peak long run. In 12:49-50 change 'od 8.3.2027' to 'od 13.10.2026; březen = doladění při MP'. Rewrite 07:113-117 in g/h.

findings.title: The KB's fueling 'lessons' come from single, confounded runs: fueling hasn't been the limit at ≤100 min so far
findings.claim: 03:32 says 'fasted, no hydration → drift' for the 11.65 km run. The stream shows almost no decoupling: HR was high from km 2, with a late start and a week after the Crete gorge hikes. The 'verified protocol' (07:104-109) came after two rest days and a ~3500 kcal celebration the evening before, a de facto carb-load. The gel can't be credited. Long runs of 86–99 min with unknown fueling show no late HR drift. So far fueling hasn't limited performance; its value until December is gut training. That makes the peach-and-nectarine breakfast (~20–25 g carbs) fine for now and too little for 2 h+ runs.
findings.recommendation: Relabel the 13.19 km protocol as 'gel tolerance test (n=1)', not proof that a gel prevents drift. For long runs ≥18 km, eat 1–1.5 g/kg (80–120 g carbs) 2–3 h before, or 40–60 g of simple carbs if leaving within 60–90 min. Keep fat and fiber low. From now on, put a one-line fueling log in the Strava description of every run ≥75 min: breakfast grams of carbs and timing, gels and minutes taken, ml drunk, sodium, GI rating 0–3. That closes 12:27 for good and makes later analyses possible.
findings.plan_change: Add a rule in 04 under 'Pravidla plánování': 'Každý běh ≥75 min: fueling log do popisu Stravy.' Reword 03:32 and 07:104 accordingly.

findings.title: The gym schedules in 09 and 04 contradict each other and the errata, and the week after return puts the first leg session in the worst spot
findings.claim: The 09 split was written before threshold work existed. It has an easy run on Saturday before the Sunday long run, which the errata forbid, and two lower sessions. The 04 templates have one lower session on Sunday afternoon after the long run, no lower session on the quality day (09's own 'ideal'), and an easy run on Monday after the long run, which the errata also forbid. The C+ template places no gym at all. Legs after the long run are acceptable at 16 km. At 18–24 km they mean lifting glycogen-depleted, with more soreness running into Tuesday's quality session. Week 1 after return adds the first lower session after ~3 weeks off right after the first long run, with DOMS peaking into the week-2 hill session. Gym sessions aren't logged in Strava, so compliance and effects can't be checked from the data.
findings.evidence: KB: 09:37-45 (split, 'So Easy run' before 'Ne Long run'), 09:84-91 (2 lower sessions better, 10–14 sets), 09:108-116 (rule 5: lower ideally right after the quality session), 04:175-184 (Po easy after Ne LR, lower only on Ne afternoon), 04:186-195 (flex easy the day after a Friday LR), 04:197-206 (C+ with no gym), 04:106-114 (Ne 19.10. LR 12 km + gym lower), 04:90 (week 2 hill repeats), errata 11:30-37, 05:105-116 (recovery runs only at 60+ km and 5–6 runs). Dataset: weekly.json gym = 0 in every week except 31.8. (one session, 5.9., id 20046482336, 50 min).
findings.recommendation: Use one unified template. With 4 runs (Oct–Nov): Po off (upper allowed); Út quality AM plus heavy lower PM (hard day stays hard, ≥4 days before the long run); St easy plus upper A; Čt off or mobility; Pá easy plus a short light lower session of 20–25 min (plyo, calf, hip; no heavy eccentrics), about 40 h before the long run; So off or upper B; Ne long run. Lower after the long run only while the long run is ≤16–17 km and felt easy; drop it from week 4 (3.11., LR 18 km). With 5 runs and 2 quality sessions (Dec, marathon block): heavy lower after Q1 on Tuesday; Friday Q2 plus at most 15 min of calf/plyo; upper Wednesday and Saturday or Monday. Monday stays off until ~50 km/4 runs. From 5 runs/55+ km, a Z1 recovery jog of 30–40 min at HR ≤137 is allowed (05:109-116). Week of 13.10.: first lower session Wednesday 15.10. PM at ~50–60 % of usual load and sets; none after the 19.10. long run. Log gym sessions in Strava, even without HR.
findings.plan_change: 04:106-114: move 'gym lower' from Ne 19.10. to St 15.10. PM at 50–60 % volume. Replace the three templates at 04:173-206 with the unified version above, gym days included, and state the Monday rule explicitly. Mark the 09:35-45 split as superseded.

findings.title: Strength content misses what a heavy runner needs most (soleus/Achilles, plyometrics, hips) and has no plan for the trips
findings.claim: The heavy compound lifts at 3–6 reps and 2–3 RIR fit the evidence for running economy. Calf work, though, is light high-rep straight-knee raises. The soleus takes several times body weight per step (modeling studies suggest ~6–8×) and the Achilles needs heavy, slow loading. There are no plyometrics, even though they improve economy and tendon stiffness. There is no hip abductor or adductor work, and no eccentric quad work despite the knee history after big descents. Programmed leg volume (~16 sets) is above 09's own 10–14 target. The trip notes are either too generic (bodyweight squats and push-ups) or wrong for skiing: rigid ski boots take the calves and Achilles out of work for 1.5 weeks just before the January return.
findings.evidence: KB: 09:65-80 (Lower A: squat 3 + RDL 3 + calves 2; Lower B: leg press 3 + leg curl 3 + single-leg bridge 2 = 16 leg sets, plus core), 09:91 (target 10–14), 09:25 (calves 12–20 reps), 09:133 (step calves 3×15–20), 09:138-140 (travel), 04:63 (Indonesia bodyweight), 04:128 ('Gym vynechat — lyže nohy pokryjí'), 03:39-40 and 10:90 (knees after 1721 m D+ on 5.7., id 19209514381). Evidence: strength plus plyometric training improves running economy by ~2–8 % (Balsalobre-Fernández 2016; Blagrove 2018; Rønnestad & Mujika 2014); strength holds for ~3 weeks of detraining (Mujika & Padilla 2000); muscle is maintained with ~1/3 of the volume if intensity stays (Bickel 2011; Spiering 2021).
findings.recommendation: Add twice a week: heavy straight-knee calf raises 3×8–12 and bent-knee (seated or soleus) raises 3×10–15 at a 3 s lowering; tibialis raises 2×15; Copenhagen plank 2×20–30 s per side; side plank with leg lift or lateral step-downs 2×10. Plyometrics once a week in October, starting at ~40–50 low-amplitude contacts (pogo hops, line hops, A-skips), building to 2×/week at 80–100 contacts by December. No drop jumps at 83 kg until tolerated. Trim leg sets to ~12/week. Indonesia (muscle won't detrain in 2.5 weeks, so train tissue capacity), 2–3× 15–20 min: single-leg calf raises straight and bent knee 3×15–25 per leg, Bulgarian split squat with backpack 3×10–12, single-leg RDL 3×10, push-ups, side and Copenhagen planks, pogo 2×20 after one run. Georgia: no heavy lower, but 2–3× 10 min of calf, soleus, tibialis and hip work. Marathon block: one heavy lower (2–3 sets, keep the load) plus one 15 min calf/plyo session; nothing heavy within 72 h of the half marathon or the 30–32 km long runs; last heavy lower ~22.4. (10 days out); race week activation only. Upper body at maintenance (~1/3 volume, heavy) until 2.5.
findings.plan_change: 04:63: replace the bodyweight list with the calf, single-leg and plyo circuit above. 04:128: replace 'Gym vynechat' with 'těžký gym vynechat; 2–3× 10 min lýtka/soleus/tibialis/kyčle'. Marathon block: add 'poslední těžký lower ~22.4.; nic těžkého 72 h před PM a LR 30–32 km'.

findings.title: Weight strategy: default to maintenance; an optional slow cut only 13.10.–23.11., and none from December
findings.claim: Losing fat helps. At a fixed aerobic capacity, 1 kg is ~1.2 % of 83 kg, worth roughly 1.5–2.5 min over a 3:30 marathon, so 3 kg ≈ 5–7 min. But that holds only if training quality is kept. One lost week or one injury costs more. Body composition is unknown, and a bodybuilder at 83 kg may already be fairly lean. The current state (N1) probably isn't a real deficit anyway. The sensible default is maintenance, letting weight drift down as volume rises. If a deliberate cut is wanted, the only window that doesn't clash with key training is the lower-intensity first half of the main block. Raising carbs will add ~1–2 kg of glycogen and water in the first week; that is not fat.
findings.evidence: KB: 01:5 (~83 kg), 12:32 (body composition unknown), 04:88-97 (weeks 1–6 = 28–52 km with one quality session; weeks 8–10 = 2 quality sessions plus long runs 22–24 km), 04:152-166 (marathon block), 07:69-71. Sensitivity: 82/83 = 1.2 % less mass, so 3:29:40 × 1.2 % ≈ 2.5 min per kg as the theoretical upper bound. Rate evidence: Garthe 2011 (0.7 % body weight/week kept lean mass and power better than 1.4 %/week). For 83 kg, 0.3–0.5 %/week = 0.25–0.4 kg/week, about a 300–450 kcal/day deficit. Each gram of glycogen binds ~3 g water; +150–250 g/day carbs gives ~+0.5–1.5 kg on the scale.
findings.recommendation: First measure body composition: DEXA or at least waist plus a consistent BIA, in mid-October. If body fat is ≤~15 %, don't cut; eat at maintenance. If it's higher and a cut is wanted: 13.10.–23.11. only, at 0.25–0.4 kg/week, taking the deficit on easy and rest days only, never on quality days, long-run days or the day before a long run. Protein 170–180 g and two heavy sessions a week keep the muscle. Maintenance from the week-7 cutback and retest (24.11.) through race day; no deficit on any trip. Hard stop by 15.2. at the latest. Stop the cut immediately on any N1 red flag, a second bad quality session, or a failed cutback. Expect +1–2 kg in race week from carb-loading; don't weigh in race week. Don't chase upper-body growth until after 2.5.
findings.plan_change: Add a weight line to 04. Main-block weeks 1–6: 'volitelně −0,25–0,4 kg/tý jen pokud BF >15 %'. From 24.11. to 2.5.: 'maintenance, žádný deficit'. Travel blocks: 'maintenance'.

findings.title: Heat plan: the homemade electrolyte is too dilute, and there's no sweat-rate test or fluid rule for the longer runs
findings.claim: The KB's heat rules (HR cap 150, early runs, short first days) are sound. The fluid and sodium part is vague. 'A pinch of salt in 500 ml' is ~250–300 mg Na/L, a third or less of typical sweat sodium and below sports drinks. The planned longest Indonesian runs (8–10 km at 6:45–7:15/km) last ~55–75 min, the point where an 83 kg runner in 30 °C and 80 % humidity approaches 2 % body-weight loss. Volcano hikes of several hours on plain water carry a hyponatremia risk. Heat acclimation fades within ~2–3 weeks after return, and its benefit in cool conditions is inconsistent, so a lower HR after return shouldn't be read as fitness. The KB already says not to speed up.
findings.evidence: KB: 04:56-65 (rules), 04:54 and 04:72 (6:45–7:15/km; 8–10 km longest run, so 54–73 min), 07:135 ('špetka soli + lžíce medu + citron do 500 ml'), 10:73-81, 04:79-80, 04:116-117. A pinch is ~0.3–0.4 g NaCl ≈ 120–160 mg Na per 500 ml ≈ 240–320 mg/L, versus sweat Na ~900–1000 mg/L (range ~450–1800), sports drinks ~400–700 mg/L, and WHO ORS ~1700 mg/L. 1/4 tsp salt ≈ 1.4 g NaCl ≈ 575 mg Na. 2 % of 83 kg = 1.66 kg; at a literature-typical 1.0–1.5 L/h sweat rate in tropical heat, that is reached in ~65–100 min (literature values, not the athlete's own).
findings.recommendation: Indonesia and Thailand: (1) Do a sweat test once, in the first week of runs (28.9.–4.10.): nude weight before and after, towel-dried; sweat L/h = (pre − post + fluid drunk)/hours. Repeat on a cool long run in November and again in spring for the race plan. (2) 60–90 min before each run: 500 ml with 300–600 mg Na. The homemade mix should be ~1/4 tsp salt + 1 tbsp honey + lemon per 500 ml. (3) Runs >45–50 min: carry 500 ml of electrolyte drink. (4) After runs: 1.25–1.5 L per kg lost, with sodium, over 2–4 h. Salt meals freely, 3–5 L/day total, pale-yellow urine. (5) Volcano hikes: 30–60 g carbs/h plus salty snacks or electrolytes; don't drink >1 L/h of plain water. The day after, follow the KB rule (04:64-65). (6) Stop and cool down at dizziness, chills or goosebumps in the heat, confusion, or when sweating stops. The HR cap of 150 may mean walking; that's fine.
findings.plan_change: 04:61 'Elektrolyty vždy': replace with the concrete dose (1/4 tsp salt per 500 ml, 300–600 mg Na before) plus 'nést 500 ml na běhy >45–50 min' and 'sweat test v týdnu 28.9.–4.10.'. Same for Thailand (04:147).

findings.title: Recovery and supplements: re-rank the priorities, get a blood panel on return, time vitamin D, handle creatine and caffeine deliberately, and add travel-illness rules
findings.claim: 08's priority table ranks sufficient energy as a fat issue. It is the #1 modifiable lever. Iron and vitamin D are untested. The risk factors are real: 83 kg with high-impact footstrike, heavy sweating in the tropics, low-iron staples (chicken breast, tvaroh, oats; no red meat or legumes in the documented menu), coffee with breakfast, and a latitude of ~49.5° N (little vitamin D made from sun Oct–Mar). Creatine is still under consideration. Starting it would add ~0.5–1.5 kg of water, which would corrupt the N1 weight audit. Caffeine is the best-evidenced race aid and isn't planned. The illness rules don't cover the likely travel scenarios: GI infections, and dengue in Indonesia, where NSAIDs are contraindicated.
findings.evidence: KB: 08:3-13 (priority #3 'tuky nízké'), 12:34 (blood tests not done), 07:8-14 (menu), 07:147-148 (creatine, vitamin D 2000–4000 IU), 12:18 (creatine 'zvážit'), 08:87-94 (neck check), 07:119 (avoid caffeinated gels at first). Iron: ferritin <30–35 µg/L is performance-relevant iron deficiency in athletes (Sim et al. 2019). Caffeine: 3 mg/kg = ~250 mg for 83 kg (ISSN 2021 position: 3–6 mg/kg ~60 min before; works in habitual users too).
findings.recommendation: (1) Re-rank 08: #1 enough energy and carbs, #2 sleep (already good), #3 load management, #4 blood work, then everything else. (2) Blood panel Thu 16.10. (rest day, morning, fasted, ≥48 h after hard training, not straight off the flight): CBC, ferritin, transferrin saturation, 25(OH)D, CRP. Because of N1, add total testosterone, TSH and fT3. Treat low ferritin with a doctor; never take iron blindly as a man. Repeat ferritin and Hb ~mid-February before the marathon block if borderline. (3) Vitamin D: the October level will be near the year's high after summer and Indonesia. Start 1000–2000 IU/day with a meal from November regardless, unless it's >100 nmol/L, and adjust by a February retest. (4) Creatine: optional. If used, start only after the 14-day audit. Treat the scale jump as water. Consider stopping ~4–6 weeks before the race (~late March) if you want the ~1 kg off; the net effect on the marathon is uncertain. (5) Caffeine: 3 mg/kg (~250 mg) ~60 min before, or ~150–200 mg before plus a 100 mg caffeinated gel at ~km 25–30. Test on an MP long run in March and at the half marathon. (6) Omega-3 and magnesium are low priority once fat is 60–70 g with fish twice a week. (7) Illness: GI infection means oral rehydration salts and no running until 24 h without symptoms and eating normally. Fever means no running until 24–48 h fever-free, then 1–2 easy days before any quality. Fever plus body or eye pain in Indonesia means see a doctor (possible dengue): paracetamol only, no ibuprofen or aspirin.

findings.title: What's working: sleep, the protein correction, strength philosophy, heat rules, and long-run durability
findings.claim: Sleep of ~8 h is the strongest recovery asset, and the KB correctly protects it (don't move runs earlier at the cost of sleep). Protein at 170–180 g (2.0–2.2 g/kg) is on target, and the errata fix stands. The strength philosophy is evidence-aligned: hybrid, heavy 3–6 reps at 2–3 RIR, cutting sets before exercises as volume rises. So are the stretching and foam-roller priorities. The heat HR cap and acclimatization rules are sensible. Long runs up to 99 min stay steady without any known fueling, so aerobic durability is a strength to build on. It doesn't need fixing.
findings.recommendation: Don't change these. Protect sleep especially around the flights (jet lag of +5–6 h eastbound) and in the marathon block. Build fueling and gym changes around the long-run durability rather than 'fixing' the long runs.
